questions.question: Which of the following is known as plastic money?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Credit Cards**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Credit cards are commonly referred to as **plastic money** because they are made of plastic and allow users to make purchases without the need for physical cash.
 
• They are financial instruments issued by banks or financial institutions, enabling users to borrow funds within a pre-approved credit limit.
 
• Credit cards provide convenience, allowing users to make **cashless transactions** both online and offline.
 
• They offer additional benefits such as **rewards points, cashback, discounts, and EMI (Equated Monthly Installment) options**, making them a preferred mode of payment for many.
 
• Unlike debit cards, credit cards allow users to pay for purchases later, offering a short-term credit period without interest, provided the balance is paid in full by the due date.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fixed Deposit (Option 1):**

 
 
• A fixed deposit (FD) is a financial instrument offered by banks where a fixed sum of money is deposited for a specific tenure to earn guaranteed interest.
 
• Fixed deposits are not cashless transaction tools but are primarily savings instruments.
 
• The interest rate on an FD is higher than a standard savings account, and premature withdrawal may attract a penalty.
 
 
 
• **Bearer Cheques (Option 3):**
 
 
• A bearer cheque is a type of cheque that is payable to the person presenting it at the bank, regardless of the name written on the cheque.
 
• It is a physical document and cannot be classified as plastic money or a cashless payment method.
 
• Bearer cheques are prone to misuse if lost or stolen as anyone holding the cheque can encash it.
 
 
 
• **Demand Drafts (Option 4):**
 
 
• A demand draft (DD) is a prepaid negotiable instrument issued by a bank, guaranteeing payment to the specified payee.
 
• Unlike credit cards, demand drafts require the payer to deposit funds in advance and are used for secure, large transactions.
 
 
 
• **Plastic Money:**
 
 
• Plastic money refers to credit cards, debit cards, prepaid cards, and other similar financial tools made of plastic that enable cashless transactions.
 
• It has gained immense popularity due to its convenience, security, and ability to support digital transactions in an increasingly cashless economy.
 
• Plastic money has significantly contributed to the global push toward digitalization and financial inclusion.

questions.question: What do we deduct from the Gross National Product to get the Net National Product?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Loss or Depreciation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Gross National Product (GNP) measures the total market value of all final goods and services produced by a country's residents in a given time period, including income earned overseas.
 
• To derive the Net National Product (NNP), the value of loss or depreciation of capital assets is subtracted from the Gross National Product.
 
• Depreciation refers to the reduction in the value of assets due to wear and tear, obsolescence, or other factors over time.
 
• Net National Product (NNP) at market price = GNP at market price - Depreciation.
 
• This adjustment ensures that the NNP reflects the true economic value generated within a country after accounting for asset losses.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: Imports**

 
 
• Imports refer to goods or services brought into a country from abroad for consumption, trade, or resale.
 
• While imports affect a country's trade balance, they are not deducted from GNP to calculate NNP. GNP includes the economic activities of citizens regardless of geographical location.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: Interim Payments**
 
 
• Interim payments are partial payments made during the course of work or a financial transaction. They are common in contractual agreements.
 
• These payments are unrelated to the calculation of NNP as they do not represent asset depreciation or economic output adjustments.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Direct Taxes**
 
 
• Direct taxes are taxes paid directly by individuals or organizations to the government, such as income tax or corporate tax.
 
• Direct taxes are not deducted from GNP to calculate NNP as they represent government revenue, not asset depreciation or loss.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: Gross National Product (GNP) and Net National Product (NNP)**
 
 
• GNP and NNP are key macroeconomic indicators used to measure a country's economic performance.
 
• GNP includes contributions from citizens and entities operating abroad, while NNP adjusts GNP by subtracting depreciation.
 
• The distinction between GNP and NNP helps economists and policymakers understand the sustainability of economic growth and the condition of national assets.

questions.question: Who was the first chairman of the Planning Commission?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jawaharlal Nehru**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• The Planning Commission was created by a resolution of the Government of India in **March 1950**, with the aim of formulating five-year plans for the country’s development.
 
• As the Prime Minister of India, Nehru held the position of chairman of the Planning Commission, reflecting his vision for economic planning and development.
 
• The Planning Commission was tasked with assessing the nation’s resources and devising strategies to achieve economic growth and social justice.
 
• Under Nehru's leadership, the first Five-Year Plan (1951–1956) emphasized agricultural development, irrigation, and energy resources.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Dr. Rajendra Prasad**

 
 
• First President of India; associated with the Constituent Assembly.
 
 
 
• **Dr. S. Radhakrishnan**
 
 
• Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan was an eminent philosopher and statesman who served as first vice president and second President of India (1962–1967).
 
• He was a distinguished academic and is widely known for promoting education in India.
 
 
 
• **M. Vishveshwaraya**
 
 
• Bharat Ratna awardee (1955); his birthday (15 September) is observed as **Engineer’s **Day.
 
• He is known for his contributions to industrialization and irrigation projects in India, including the construction of the Krishna Raja Sagara Dam.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Planning Commission**

 
 
• The Planning Commission was a central institution in India responsible for formulating Five-Year Plans to promote economic development.
 
• It was replaced by the **NITI Aayog** in 2015 to focus on cooperative federalism and sustainable development goals.
 
• The Planning Commission played a crucial role in shaping India’s economic policies during its existence.

questions.question: Which of the following deals with economic offences?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**PATA**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **PATA (Prevention of Anti-Social Activities Act)** is a legislative framework aimed at preventing and dealing with economic offences.
 
• Economic offences generally include crimes such as tax evasion, money laundering, financial fraud, and other white-collar crimes that destabilize the economy.
 
• PATA provides a legal mechanism to curb and prevent such offences by enabling the authorities to take strict and preventive actions.
 
• The act focuses on regulating activities that could lead to financial instability or exploitation of economic resources.
 
• Economic offences are considered a critical aspect of governance as they impact economic growth and public trust in financial systems.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **POTA (Prevention of Terrorism Act):**

 
 
• POTA was enacted in 2002 to combat terrorism in India.
 
• The law provided law enforcement agencies with special powers to deal with terrorist activities.
 
• It allowed preventive detention and provided stricter measures to curb terrorism.
 
• POTA was repealed in 2004 due to concerns over its misuse.
 
 
 
• **TADA (Terrorist and Disruptive Activities Act):**
 
 
• TADA was introduced in 1985 to address terrorist activities and disruptive practices in India.
 
• The act allowed for enhanced investigative powers for law enforcement agencies.
 
• It faced criticism for being draconian and was allowed to lapse in 1995.
 
 
 
• **MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act):**
 
 
• MISA was enacted in 1971 during the period of internal security threats in India.
 
• It allowed preventive detention and was primarily used during the Emergency period (1975–1977).
 
• The act was heavily criticized for its misuse and was repealed in 1977.

questions.question: Which country is following one party system?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**China**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• China follows a **one-party system**, with the Communist Party of China (CPC) as the sole governing political party.
 
• The Communist Party of China was founded in 1921 and has maintained its dominance since the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
 
• In the one-party system, other political parties exist but operate under the leadership and guidance of the CPC, with limited autonomy.
 
• The Chinese political system is structured around the leadership of the CPC, with no formal opposition parties allowed to challenge its authority.
 
• The CPC's governance aims to promote socialism with Chinese characteristics, focusing on centralized planning and control of the economy and society.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chile**

 
 
• Chile follows a **multi-party system** where multiple political parties participate in elections and governance.
 
• The political system in Chile operates under a democratic framework, with regular elections held to choose representatives for various levels of government.
 
• Chile's political system includes both left-wing and right-wing parties, promoting a pluralistic and competitive political environment.
 
 
 
• **Russia**
 
 
• Russia has a **dominant-party system**, with the United Russia party holding significant power, but other political parties are permitted to exist.
 
• Although opposition parties exist, critics argue that the political system in Russia is highly centralized, with limited scope for genuine opposition.
 
• The president, who holds extensive powers, plays a central role in Russian politics, influencing the overall functioning of the system.
 
 
 
• **Spain**
 
 
• Spain is a **parliamentary constitutional monarchy** with a multi-party system.
 
• The political system in Spain includes several major parties, such as the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) and the People's Party (PP), along with regional parties.
 
• Spain's democracy allows for free and fair elections, where political parties compete for representation in the Cortes Generales (the Spanish Parliament).
 
 
 
• **Concept of One-Party System**
 
 
• In a one-party system, a single political party holds exclusive control over the government, with no competition allowed from other parties.
 
• This system is often criticized for limiting political freedom and suppressing dissent, as opposition parties are either banned or heavily restricted.
 
• Countries like North Korea, Cuba, and China are examples of nations following the one-party system.

questions.question: The essential feature of democracy is giving prominence to the ____
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Citizen**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Democracy is a form of government in which the **citizens are the ultimate source of political power**.
 
• The cornerstone of democracy is the concept of popular sovereignty, meaning **the power lies with the people**, who exercise their rights through elections and active participation in governance.
 
• Citizens in a democracy have **basic rights such as freedom of speech, association, and equality**, which enable them to express their opinions and influence decision-making processes.
 
• **Universal adult suffrage** is a key characteristic of democracy, granting every adult citizen the right to vote regardless of gender, race, or socioeconomic status.
 
• Democratic societies emphasize transparency and accountability, ensuring that the government operates in the interest of the citizens.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Civil Organisation**

 
 
• Civil organizations play an important role in strengthening democracy by promoting civic engagement, advocating for social justice, and providing a platform for marginalized groups.
 
• While civil organizations contribute to democratic processes, they are not the ultimate source of power in a democracy—that role belongs to the citizens.
 
• Examples include NGOs, advocacy groups, and community-based organizations that work towards policy reforms and social development.
 
 
 
• **Judiciary**
 
 
• The judiciary is a critical institution in a democracy, responsible for upholding the rule of law and ensuring justice.
 
• It acts as an independent body that checks the powers of the executive and legislature, safeguarding the rights of citizens.
 
• While the judiciary is vital for maintaining democratic principles, it does not hold the primary power in a democracy, as that resides with the people.
 
 
 
• **Executives**
 
 
• The executive branch of government implements laws and policies created by the legislature.
 
• It includes the president, prime minister, and other government officials who manage the day-to-day administration of the country.
 
• In a democracy, executives derive their authority from the mandate given by the citizens through elections.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• India's Constitution envisages three types of emergencies under Articles 352, 356, and 360.
 
• **National Emergency** (Article 352): Declared due to war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. It impacts the entire nation or a part of it.
 
• **State Emergency** (President’s Rule, Article 356): Imposed if a state’s governance fails to follow constitutional provisions.
 
• **Financial Emergency** (Article 360): Declared when the financial stability of India or any part of its territory is threatened.
 
• Each emergency type requires parliamentary approval within a stipulated timeframe and has distinct implications on governance and fundamental rights.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Emergency:**

 
 
• The provision for emergencies is covered under Part XVIII of the Indian Constitution, titled "**Emergency Provisions**."
 
• Emergency provisions empower the central government to act decisively in extraordinary circumstances to safeguard national security, governance, and financial stability.
 
• These provisions significantly alter the distribution of powers between the center and states and can impact fundamental rights.
 
• National Emergency has been imposed three times:** 1962, 1971, and 1975.**

questions.question: Under which article of the Indian Constitution can the Central Government direct the State Governments?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 256**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 256** of the Indian Constitution states that the executive power of every state must be exercised to ensure compliance with the laws made by Parliament and any existing laws applicable to that state.
 
• The Central Government can issue directions to State Governments to ensure the implementation of parliamentary laws and compliance with constitutional provisions.
 
• This article helps maintain the unitary feature of the Indian Constitution while ensuring cooperation between the Union and the States.
 
• Failure of a state to comply with these directions can invoke the provisions of Article 356, which allows the imposition of President's Rule in the state.
 
• Article 256 ensures that the laws enacted by the Parliament are uniformly implemented across all states, supporting the principle of federal governance in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 263**:

 
 
• This article provides for the establishment of an Inter-State Council by the President of India.
 
• The council is meant to investigate and discuss subjects of common interest between the Union and the States or among the States themselves.
 
• It is a constitutional body aimed at fostering coordination and cooperation between different levels of government in the federal structure.
 
 
 
• **Article 356**:
 
 
• Under this article, the President can impose President's Rule in a state if the constitutional machinery of the state breaks down.
 
• This power is exercised based on the recommendation of the Governor of the concerned state.
 
• It is also referred to as "State Emergency" or "Constitutional Emergency."
 
 
 
• **Article 370**:
 
 
• Article 370 provided special autonomous status to the state of Jammu and Kashmir.
 
• However, this article was effectively abrogated on August 5, 2019, through a Presidential Order and the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Act, 2019.
 
• As a result, Jammu and Kashmir was reorganized into two Union Territories: Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

questions.question: Which one of the following dynasties was founded by Bimbisara?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Haryanka**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Haryanka dynasty was founded by **Bimbisara**, who ruled from 544 BCE to 492 BCE in Magadha (modern-day Bihar).
 
• Bimbisara was considered the architect of the Magadhan Empire and expanded his kingdom through strategic marriages and diplomacy.
 
• The Haryanka dynasty is one of the earliest dynasties of the Indian subcontinent, which laid the foundation for subsequent powerful empires.
 
• Bimbisara was succeeded by his son Ajatashatru, who played a key role in further expanding the Magadhan Empire.
 
• The dynasty is known for its association with Buddhism and Jainism, as Bimbisara was a patron of Gautama Buddha and also supported Jain tirthankaras.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nanda Dynasty**

 
 
• The Nanda dynasty preceded the Mauryan Empire and was founded by Mahapadma Nanda in the 4th century BCE.
 
• The Nandas were known for their immense wealth and a large standing army, which was among the largest in ancient India.
 
• This dynasty was later overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya, who established the Mauryan Empire.
 
 
 
• **Maurya Dynasty**
 
 
• The Maurya dynasty was founded by Chandragupta Maurya in 321 BCE with the guidance of his advisor Chanakya (Kautilya).
 
• The Mauryan Empire is considered one of the largest and most powerful empires in ancient India, with rulers like Ashoka who embraced and promoted Buddhism.
 
• It marked the unification of most of the Indian subcontinent under a central administration.
 
 
 
• **Gupta Dynasty**
 
 
• The Gupta dynasty was established by Sri Gupta in the early 4th century CE and is often referred to as the "Golden Age" of India.
 
• Famous rulers like Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, and Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) contributed to advancements in science, art, and literature.
 
• The period saw significant achievements in mathematics, astronomy, and architecture, including the works of Aryabhata and Kalidasa.

questions.question: What was the another name of Quit India Movement?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**August Kranti**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Quit India Movement, launched on **8 August 1942**, is also known as the **August Kranti**.
 
• It was initiated by the Indian National Congress under the leadership of **Mahatma Gandhi** to demand an end to British rule in India.
 
• The slogan "**Do or Die**" was given by Mahatma Gandhi during this movement, urging Indians to fight until independence was achieved.
 
• The movement began with **mass protests and civil disobedience** across the country, marking a significant phase in India’s struggle for independence.
 
• The Quit India Movement is considered a turning point that compelled the British to seriously consider granting independence to India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Non-Cooperation Movement**

 
 
• Launched in **1920** by Mahatma Gandhi, the Non-Cooperation Movement aimed to resist British rule in India through non-violent means.
 
• It involved boycotting British goods, institutions, titles, and services.
 
• It marked the first mass movement under Gandhi’s leadership and laid the foundation for future movements like Civil Disobedience.
 
• The movement was withdrawn in 1922 after the **Chauri Chaura incident**, where violence erupted, leading to the death of policemen.
 
 
 
• **Civil Disobedience Movement**
 
 
• Launched in **1930**, this movement involved deliberately breaking British laws as a form of protest.
 
• The **Dandi March**, led by Mahatma Gandhi, was a symbolic beginning of the movement, where Gandhi broke the salt laws imposed by the British.
 
• It aimed at achieving complete independence (Purna Swaraj) and saw mass participation across the country.
 
• The movement was significant in weakening British authority and showcasing Indian unity against colonial rule.

__
 
• The Surat session of the Indian National Congress was held in **1906**.
 
• During this session, the Indian National Congress split into two factions—**Moderates** and **Extremists**.
 
• The split occurred due to ideological differences between the two groups regarding the methods to achieve self-rule.
 
• The Moderates, led by leaders like **Gopal Krishna Gokhale**, advocated constitutional methods, gradual reforms, and dialogue with the British government.
 
• The Extremists, led by leaders like **Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Lala Lajpat Rai**, supported more radical measures and mass mobilization to push for complete independence.
 
• The split weakened the Congress temporarily but laid the groundwork for more assertive political movements later.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lahore, 1909:**

 
 
• The Lahore session of 1909 was significant as it occurred during the time when the Morley-Minto reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909) were introduced.
 
• These reforms introduced separate electorates for Muslims, which sowed seeds of communalism in Indian politics.
 
• While this session did not involve a split, it reflected the growing unrest among Indians toward British policies.
 
 
 
• **Madras, 1908:**
 
 
• The Madras session was not directly linked to the split of the Congress but was significant for discussing political strategies.
 
• This session focused on the Swadeshi movement and the boycott of British goods as a form of protest.** **

• **Indian National Congress**:

 
 
• The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 by A.O. Hume to provide a platform for Indians to discuss their grievances against British rule.
 
• Over time, ideological differences emerged among its members, leading to the split in 1906.
 
• Despite the split, the Congress played a pivotal role in India's freedom struggle, uniting various factions and ideologies over time.

questions.question: Where did the development of miniature paintings of Indian heritage NOT happen at the followings?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Junagarh, located in Gujarat, is historically significant for its association with ancient Indian architecture and heritage, but it is **not known for the development of miniature paintings**.
 
• Miniature painting traditions in India primarily flourished in regions like Rajasthan, Punjab Hills, and Mughal courts, but Junagarh did not contribute notably to this art form.
 
• The miniature painting style developed under royal patronage and reflected regional influences, but Junagarh’s cultural contributions focused more on inscriptions, rock-cut architecture, and religious developments.
 
• Junagarh is famous for monuments like the **Uparkot Fort and the Girnar Hills**, which are known for their historical significance rather than artistic movements like miniature paintings.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mewar:**

 
 
• Mewar is one of the most notable centers for the development of miniature paintings in India, particularly during the 16th and 17th centuries.
 
• The Mewar style is characterized by bold lines, bright colors, and depictions of heroic themes, court scenes, and religious motifs.
 
• Mewar paintings often portray stories from the** Ramayana, Mahabharata, and Krishna Leela **with intricate detailing.
 
 
 
• **Kishangarh:**
 
 
• Kishangarh is renowned for its contribution to Indian miniature art, especially the depiction of Radha and Krishna in the "Bani Thani" style.
 
• The Kishangarh style is known for its elongated features, detailed expressions, and romantic themes.
 
• It was developed under the patronage of **Raja Savant Singh**, who was a significant supporter of art and culture.
 
 
 
• **Bundi:**
 
 
• Bundi is famous for its unique miniature paintings, which reflect a blend of** Mughal and indigenous Rajasthani styles.**
 
• Bundi paintings are known for their vibrant colors, naturalistic depictions, and intricate designs, often showcasing flora, fauna, and human figures.
 
• The subjects of Bundi paintings often include courtly scenes, hunting expeditions, and mythical narratives.

questions.question: In which state is located the Lipulekh Pass?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Uttarakhand**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Lipulekh Pass** is located in the state of **Uttarakhand, India**, specifically in the Pithoragarh district near the India-China border.
 
• It serves as a strategic border point connecting **India, Nepal, and China**, making it geopolitically significant.
 
• The Lipulekh Pass is part of the ancient **trade route to Tibet** and is also used by pilgrims traveling to **Kailash Mansarovar**.
 
• It lies at an altitude of approximately **5,200 meters (17,060 feet)** above sea level in the Himalayan region.
 
• This pass has been a point of contention between **India and Nepal**, as both countries claim it as part of their territory.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: Sikkim**

 
 
• Sikkim is home to several important mountain passes, such as **Nathu La** and **Jelep La**, which connect India with Tibet (China).
 
• Nathu La is a significant pass used for trade and is located at an altitude of approximately 4,310 meters.
 
• Jelep La, situated at an altitude of about 4,267 meters, was historically used as a trade route between India and Tibet.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: Himachal Pradesh**
 
 
• Himachal Pradesh features important passes such as **Rohtang Pass, Baralacha La, and Kunzum Pass**.
 
• Rohtang Pass, located near Manali, is a famous tourist destination at an altitude of 3,978 meters.
 
• Baralacha La connects Lahaul and Ladakh and lies at an altitude of 4,890 meters.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Jammu and Kashmir**
 
 
• Jammu and Kashmir features crucial passes like **Zoji La, Banihal Pass, and Khardung La**.
 
• Zoji La is a vital link between Srinagar and Leh, situated at an altitude of 3,528 meters.
 
• Khardung La is one of the highest motorable passes in the world, located at an altitude of 5,359 meters.

questions.question: Which one of the following lakes a salt water lake?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sambhar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Sambhar Lake** is India's largest inland saltwater lake located in the state of Rajasthan.
 
• The lake is a major source of salt production in India, contributing significantly to the country's salt economy.
 
• Sambhar Lake covers an area of approximately **200 square kilometers** and is surrounded by the Aravalli hills.
 
• The lake is fed by several seasonal rivers such as the **Medtha, Rupangarh, Khari, Mantha, Khandel, and Samod**.
 
• Sambhar Lake is a wetland of international importance under the **Ramsar Convention.**
 
• The lake is also a habitat for migratory birds, including flamingos, pelicans, and storks, making it an important ecological zone.

questions.question: Which of the following region receives rainfall by Western Disturbances?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Punjab**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Western Disturbances are extratropical storms originating in the Mediterranean region that bring sudden winter rainfall to the northwestern parts of India, including Punjab.
 
• Punjab experiences rainfall during the winter months (December to February) due to the influence of these Western Disturbances.
 
• The rainfall brought by Western Disturbances is crucial for the cultivation of rabi crops, such as wheat, in Punjab.
 
• These disturbances are carried eastward by westerly winds and typically affect northern India, including Punjab, Haryana, and western Uttar Pradesh.
 
• The Himalayan region plays a significant role in intensifying these disturbances, leading to precipitation in Punjab and other northwestern states.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kerala**

 
 
• Kerala primarily receives rainfall due to the southwest monsoon, which occurs between June and September.
 
• The state is also affected by the northeast monsoon (October to November), contributing to its overall high rainfall levels.
 
• Western Disturbances do not significantly impact Kerala, as they primarily affect the northern and northwestern parts of India.
 
 
 
• **Tamil Nadu**
 
 
• Tamil Nadu receives most of its rainfall during the northeast monsoon season (October to December).
 
• It lies in the rain shadow region of the Western Ghats, which blocks the southwest monsoon winds, resulting in lesser rainfall during that season.
 
• Western Disturbances have no significant influence on Tamil Nadu's weather patterns.
 
 
 
• **Karnataka**
 
 
• Karnataka, particularly its coastal regions, experiences heavy rainfall during the southwest monsoon season (June to September).
 
• The interior regions of Karnataka, including the northern and southern plateaus, receive moderate rainfall during the monsoon.
 
• Western Disturbances do not affect Karnataka, as their impact is limited to northern and northwestern India.
 
 
 
• **Western Disturbances**
 
 
• Western Disturbances are low-pressure systems originating in the Mediterranean and Atlantic regions.
 
• They bring significant rainfall and snowfall to the Himalayan region and the plains of northern India during winter.
 
• They are critical for the rabi crop cycle and contribute to the water availability in the region.

questions.question: Which of the following receives the first monsoon in summer?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Western Ghats**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Western Ghats receive the first monsoon rainfall in India during the summer season due to their geographical location and proximity to the Arabian Sea.
 
• When the southwest monsoon winds hit the western coast of India, the Western Ghats act as a barrier, forcing the moist winds to rise and condense, resulting in heavy rainfall.
 
• This region experiences orographic rainfall, where the moist air is lifted over the mountainous terrain, leading to precipitation.
 
• The Western Ghats are known for their lush greenery and biodiversity, heavily influenced by the abundant rainfall during the monsoon season.
 
• Key areas like Kerala and Karnataka, which are part of the Western Ghats, are among the first regions to receive the monsoon rains in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Himalayas**

 
 
• The Himalayas do not receive the first monsoon rains; rather, they play a crucial role in preventing the monsoon winds from escaping northward.
 
• They act as a climatic barrier, aiding in the formation of monsoon winds by trapping moisture-laden clouds over India.
 
• The northern plains below the Himalayas experience rainfall due to monsoon winds deflected by the mountain range.
 
 
 
• **Meghalaya Plateau**
 
 
• The Meghalaya Plateau receives heavy rainfall during the monsoon, especially in areas like Cherrapunji and Mawsynram, which are among the wettest places on Earth.
 
• However, it does not receive the first monsoon rains; these arrive after the Western Ghats experience rainfall.
 
• The plateau receives rainfall due to its elevation and position relative to monsoon winds, resulting in orographic precipitation.
 
 
 
• **Eastern Ghats**
 
 
• The Eastern Ghats do not receive the first monsoon rains as they are located on the eastern side of India, away from the direct path of the southwest monsoon winds.
 
• Rainfall in the Eastern Ghats is relatively lower compared to the Western Ghats, and it is influenced by the northeast monsoon during the later part of the year.
 
• The Eastern Ghats also receive sporadic rainfall from cyclonic storms originating in the Bay of Bengal.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the fundamental quantities in physics?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Weight**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Fundamental quantities are the physical quantities that are independent and cannot be expressed in terms of other physical quantities.
 
• The fundamental quantities in physics include **Time, Length, Mass, Electric Current, Temperature, Amount of Substance, and Luminous Intensity**.
 
• Weight is **not a fundamental quantity**; it is a derived quantity as it depends on mass and acceleration due to gravity (Weight = Mass × Gravity).
 
• Weight is measured in newtons (N), whereas mass is a fundamental quantity measured in kilograms (kg).
 
• SI units of fundamental quantities are universally accepted, forming the basis for all physical measurements.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Time:**

 
 
• Time is a fundamental quantity in physics, represented in the SI unit **second (s)**.
 
• It is used to measure the duration of events or intervals between them.
 
• Time is independent of other physical quantities and is one of the seven fundamental quantities.
 
 
 
• **Length:**
 
 
• Length is another fundamental quantity, and its SI unit is the **meter (m)**.
 
• It is used to measure the distance between two points or the extent of an object.
 
• All other measurements of distance, area, and volume are derived from length.
 
 
 
• **Mass:**
 
 
• Mass is a fundamental quantity and is measured in the SI unit **kilogram (kg)**.
 
• It refers to the amount of matter contained in an object, which remains constant regardless of location.
 
• Mass is different from weight, which changes with gravitational force.
 
 
 
• **Weight:**
 
 
• Weight is a derived quantity and varies depending on the gravitational field strength of the location.
 
• It is calculated using the formula **Weight = Mass × Gravitational Acceleration (g)**.
 
• Its SI unit is the newton (N), and it is not considered a fundamental quantity in physics.

questions.question: Which of the following produces more severe burns?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Steam**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Steam causes more severe burns than boiling water** because steam contains latent heat in addition to the heat of boiling water.
 
• When steam comes into contact with the skin, it condenses into water, releasing a large amount of latent heat energy, making burns more severe.
 
• The latent heat of vaporization of water is approximately 540 calories per gram, which is released during condensation, adding to the energy transferred to the skin.
 
• Steam is at a higher energy state compared to boiling water at the same temperature (100°C), making it more damaging upon contact.
 
• Burns caused by steam penetrate deeper into the skin tissues, often leading to second-degree or third-degree burns.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Boiling Water:**

 
 
• Boiling water at 100°C can cause burns but is less severe compared to steam at the same temperature.
 
• It lacks the additional latent heat energy that steam possesses, making its thermal energy transfer lower.
 
• It primarily causes superficial burns or first-degree burns if exposure is limited.
 
 
 
• **Hot Air:**
 
 
• Hot air has a lower heat capacity compared to water or steam, so its ability to cause burns is significantly reduced.
 
• Even at higher temperatures, the thermal conductivity of air is low, meaning it transfers heat to the skin less efficiently.
 
• Prolonged exposure to hot air can cause dehydration and skin irritation, but severe burns are less common.
 
 
 
• **Sun Rays:**
 
 
• Sun rays primarily cause burns through ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which affects the outer layer of the skin.
 
• They typically cause first-degree burns, commonly referred to as sunburn, which can result in redness, pain, and peeling of the skin.
 
• Prolonged UV exposure can damage DNA and increase the risk of skin cancer, but it does not penetrate as deeply as thermal burns caused by steam or boiling water.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• Burns are **categorized **into first, second, and third degrees based on their **severity and depth.**
 
• The severity of burns depends on the source of heat, its temperature, and the duration of contact.
 
• Latent heat plays a crucial role in determining the severity of burns caused by substances like steam, which carry additional energy compared to their liquid or solid states.

questions.question: Which of the following compound is responsible for the formation of kidney stones?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Calcium Oxalate**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Calcium oxalate is the most common compound responsible for the formation of kidney stones (approximately 80% of all cases).
 
• Kidney stones form when calcium combines with oxalate, a naturally occurring substance found in certain foods like spinach, nuts, and tea.
 
• Factors such as dehydration, excessive consumption of oxalate-rich foods, and genetic predisposition increase the risk of calcium oxalate stone formation.
 
• Calcium oxalate stones can vary in size and shape, ranging from small grains to larger stones that obstruct the urinary tract.
 
• Preventive measures include adequate hydration, reduction of oxalate-rich food intake, and maintaining a balanced diet low in salt and animal protein.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sodium Chloride:**

 
 
• While sodium chloride itself is not directly responsible for kidney stone formation, excessive salt intake can increase calcium levels in the urine, which may contribute to stone development.
 
• High sodium intake reduces calcium reabsorption in the kidneys, leading to hypercalciuria, a risk factor for calcium-based stones.
 
 
 
• **Silicates:**
 
 
• Silicate compounds are not typically associated with kidney stone formation in humans.
 
• Silicate-based kidney stones are extremely rare and are usually linked to environmental or occupational exposure to silicates.
 
 
 
• **Calcium Bicarbonate:**
 
 
• Calcium bicarbonate is not directly linked to kidney stone formation.
 
• However, high levels of calcium in the diet can combine with oxalate or phosphate to form stones, depending on urinary conditions.
 
• Maintaining balanced levels of calcium in the diet is recommended to prevent stone formation.

questions.question: Which among the following kinds of lenses are used to treat Astigmatism?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cylindrical Lens**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Astigmatism** is a common refractive error caused by an irregular curvature of the cornea or lens, resulting in blurred or distorted vision.
 
• **Cylindrical lenses** are specifically designed to correct astigmatism by compensating for the uneven curvature of the eye's cornea or lens.
 
• These lenses have different curvatures in two perpendicular directions, allowing them to focus light properly onto the retina.
 
• Cylindrical lenses are oriented at specific angles depending on the axis of astigmatism, ensuring precise correction of the refractive error.
 
• Using cylindrical lenses improves vision clarity and reduces symptoms such as eye strain and headaches caused by uncorrected astigmatism.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: Concave Lens**

 
 
• Concave lenses are commonly used to correct **myopia (nearsightedness)**, a condition where distant objects appear blurry.
 
• These lenses are thinner at the center and thicker at the edges, causing light rays to diverge before entering the eye.
 
• Concave lenses are not suitable for treating astigmatism, as they address a different type of refractive error.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: Convex Lens**
 
 
• Convex lenses are used to correct **hyperopia (farsightedness)**, a condition where nearby objects appear blurry.
 
• These lenses are thicker at the center and thinner at the edges, causing light rays to converge and focus correctly on the retina.
 
• Convex lenses do not help with astigmatism, as they do not address the irregular curvature of the cornea or lens.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: Bifocal Lens**
 
 
• Bifocal lenses are designed to correct **presbyopia**, a condition where the eye's ability to focus on nearby objects decreases with age.
 
• These lenses contain two optical powers: one for distance vision and another for near vision.
 
• Bifocal lenses are not suitable for correcting astigmatism, as they are not designed to compensate for irregular corneal curvature.

questions.question: The most malleable metal is _________.

The correct answer is __**Gold**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Gold** is the most malleable metal, meaning it can be hammered or pressed into thin sheets without breaking.
 
• A single gram of gold can be stretched into a sheet of one square meter or drawn into a wire up to 2 kilometers long.
 
• This property makes gold highly valuable for applications such as jewelry, electronics, and other industries requiring fine, intricate designs.
 
• The malleability of gold is due to its atomic structure, where atoms can slide over each other without breaking bonds.
 
• Gold also exhibits excellent ductility, corrosion resistance, and electrical conductivity, further enhancing its usability across various fields.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Platinum:**

 
 
• Platinum is a dense, malleable, and ductile metal, but its malleability is less than that of gold.
 
• It is widely used in catalytic converters, jewelry, and industrial applications due to its corrosion resistance and high melting point.
 
• Platinum is rarer than gold and is considered a precious metal, but it is not the most malleable.
 
 
 
• **Silver:**
 
 
• Silver is highly malleable and ductile but ranks below gold in terms of malleability.
 
• It is extensively used in jewelry, coinage, photography, and electronics due to its excellent conductivity and reflectivity.
 
• Silver tarnishes when exposed to air due to the formation of silver sulfide.
 
 
 
• **Iron:**
 
 
• Iron is not highly malleable compared to precious metals like gold and silver.
 
• Its malleability increases at high temperatures, making it suitable for forging and industrial purposes.
 
• Iron is primarily used in construction, manufacturing, and tools due to its strength and abundance.
 
 
 
• **Malleability in Metals:**
 
 
• Malleability is the ability of a material to deform under compressive stress and form thin sheets.
 
• It is influenced by the atomic structure and bonding of the material.
 
• Gold is considered the benchmark for malleability among all metals.

questions.question: Which of the following gas is used in manufacturing of vanaspati ghee from vegetable oil?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hydrogen**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Hydrogen gas is used in the manufacturing of vanaspati ghee through the process of hydrogenation.
 
• Hydrogenation is a chemical process where hydrogen is added to liquid vegetable oils to convert them into solid or semi-solid fats.
 
• During hydrogenation, unsaturated fats present in vegetable oils react with hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst, typically nickel, to form saturated fats.
 
• This process increases the melting point of the oil and gives vanaspati ghee its semi-solid texture.
 
• The use of hydrogen ensures the product remains stable for storage and has an extended shelf life.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Helium:**

 
 
• Helium is a noble gas and does not participate in chemical reactions like hydrogenation due to its inert nature.
 
• It is commonly used in applications such as cryogenics, as a protective gas in welding, and in medical imaging (e.g., MRI machines).
 
 
 
• **Oxygen:**
 
 
• Oxygen is essential for combustion and respiration but is not used in hydrogenation processes.
 
• In industrial applications, oxygen is used for steel manufacturing, water treatment, and as an oxidizing agent in chemical reactions.
 
 
 
• **Nitrogen:**
 
 
• Nitrogen is an inert gas commonly used in food packaging to prevent oxidation and spoilage.
 
• It is also utilized in industries for creating inert atmospheres during chemical processes but does not play a role in hydrogenation.
 
 
 
• **Hydrogenation Process:**
 
 
• Hydrogenation is a widely used industrial process to alter the physical properties of oils and fats for use in products like margarine, shortening, and vanaspati ghee.
 
• The process involves the use of high pressure, heat, and a metal catalyst to ensure the reaction occurs efficiently.
 
• While hydrogenation improves texture and stability, excessive consumption of hydrogenated fats can lead to health issues due to trans-fat formation.

questions.question: Which Layer of the atmosphere also called the Ozonosphere?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Stratosphere**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Stratosphere is the second layer of Earth’s atmosphere, located above the Troposphere and below the Mesosphere, extending from about 10 to 50 kilometers (6 to 31 miles) above sea level.
 
• It contains the Ozone Layer, also referred to as the Ozonosphere, which plays a critical role in absorbing and blocking the sun’s harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation.
 
• The Ozone Layer in the Stratosphere is vital for life on Earth as it prevents excessive exposure to UV rays that can cause health issues like skin cancer, cataracts, and immune suppression.
 
• The temperature in the Stratosphere increases with altitude due to the absorption of UV radiation by ozone molecules, making it a distinct feature of this layer.
 
• Aircraft often fly in the lower Stratosphere to avoid turbulence found in the Troposphere and to take advantage of the stable weather conditions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Troposphere:**

 
 
• The Troposphere is the lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere and extends up to 8-15 kilometers (5-9 miles) above sea level.
 
• It is where most weather phenomena, such as clouds, rain, and storms, occur due to the presence of water vapor and significant temperature variations.
 
• The temperature in the Troposphere decreases with altitude, and it contains approximately 75% of the atmosphere’s total mass.
 
 
 
• **Mesosphere:**
 
 
• The Mesosphere lies above the Stratosphere and extends from about 50 to 85 kilometers (31 to 53 miles) above Earth’s surface.
 
• In this layer, temperatures decrease with altitude, reaching the coldest temperatures in the atmosphere.
 
• The Mesosphere is also where meteoroids burn up upon entering Earth’s atmosphere, creating visible streaks known as meteors.
 
 
 
• **Ozone Layer (Ozonosphere):**
 
 
• The Ozone Layer is a high concentration of ozone (O3) molecules located primarily in the Stratosphere, between 15 and 35 kilometers (9 to 22 miles) above sea level.
 
• It absorbs the majority of the sun’s harmful ultraviolet-B (UV-B) and ultraviolet-C (UV-C) radiation.
 
• Depletion of the Ozone Layer, caused by substances like chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), poses a significant environmental challenge. Efforts like the Montreal Protocol aim to reduce ozone-depleting substances.

questions.question: Mission Indradhanush is related with ___________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Children Vaccination**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Mission Indradhanush** is a flagship program launched by the Government of India in December 2014 to ensure the complete immunization of children and pregnant women.
 
• The program aims to vaccinate children against **seven vaccine-preventable diseases**, namely Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Tuberculosis, Polio, Measles, and Hepatitis B.
 
• It was later expanded under the **Intensified Mission Indradhanush (IMI)** to include vaccines for newer diseases such as Japanese Encephalitis, Haemophilus Influenzae type B, Rotavirus, and Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines.
